front_blocks.md: Define **enzyme**.

back_blocks.md: An **enzyme** is a **biological catalyst** that increases the **rate** of a reaction and remains **unchanged** at the end of the reaction.

cards.front_md: Define **enzyme**.
cards.back_md: An **enzyme** is a **biological catalyst** that increases the **rate** of a reaction and remains **unchanged** at the end of the reaction.

front_blocks.md: What type of protein are all enzymes?

back_blocks.md: All enzymes are **globular proteins**.

cards.front_md: What type of protein are all enzymes?
cards.back_md: All enzymes are **globular proteins**.

front_blocks.md: Define **intracellular enzyme**.

back_blocks.md: An **intracellular enzyme** catalyses reactions **inside** the cell in which it is made.

cards.front_md: Define **intracellular enzyme**.
cards.back_md: An **intracellular enzyme** catalyses reactions **inside** the cell in which it is made.

front_blocks.md: Define **extracellular enzyme**.

back_blocks.md: An **extracellular enzyme** is **secreted** from the cell to catalyse reactions **outside** it.

cards.front_md: Define **extracellular enzyme**.
cards.back_md: An **extracellular enzyme** is **secreted** from the cell to catalyse reactions **outside** it.

front_blocks.md: Give one example of an **extracellular enzyme** and where it acts.

back_blocks.md: One example is **amylase**, which is secreted into the gut, where it digests **starch** outside cells.

cards.front_md: Give one example of an **extracellular enzyme** and where it acts.
cards.back_md: One example is **amylase**, which is secreted into the gut, where it digests **starch** outside cells.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Enzymes are used up during the reactions they catalyse.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Enzymes remain **unchanged** at the end of a reaction and can be **reused**.

front_blocks.md: Define **active site**.

back_blocks.md: A region on an enzyme with a **specific shape** to which the **substrate binds**.

cards.front_md: Define **active site**.
cards.back_md: A region on an enzyme with a **specific shape** to which the **substrate binds**.

front_blocks.md: Define **enzyme-substrate complex**.

back_blocks.md: The structure formed when a **substrate binds** to the **active site** of an enzyme.

cards.front_md: Define **enzyme-substrate complex**.
cards.back_md: The structure formed when a **substrate binds** to the **active site** of an enzyme.

front_blocks.md: Define **activation energy**.

back_blocks.md: The **minimum energy** needed for a reaction to take place.

cards.front_md: Define **activation energy**.
cards.back_md: The **minimum energy** needed for a reaction to take place.

front_blocks.md: How do enzymes speed up reactions?

back_blocks.md: They **lower the activation energy** of the reaction.

cards.front_md: How do enzymes speed up reactions?
cards.back_md: They **lower the activation energy** of the reaction.

front_blocks.md: What is meant by enzyme **specificity**?

back_blocks.md: Each enzyme catalyses only **one type of reaction**, because its **active site** is **complementary** to only one **substrate**.

cards.front_md: What is meant by enzyme **specificity**?
cards.back_md: Each enzyme catalyses only **one type of reaction**, because its **active site** is **complementary** to only one **substrate**.

front_blocks.md: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the <u>      </u> energy.

back_blocks.md: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the **activation** energy.

cards.back_md: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the **activation** energy.

front_blocks.md: Why is an enzyme **specific** to only one substrate?

back_blocks.md: The **shape** of its **active site** is **complementary** to only that substrate's shape.

cards.front_md: Why is an enzyme **specific** to only one substrate?
cards.back_md: The **shape** of its **active site** is **complementary** to only that substrate's shape.

front_blocks.md: Describe the **lock-and-key hypothesis** of enzyme action.

back_blocks.md: The **active site** has a **rigid, fixed shape** that is **complementary** to only one substrate.
The substrate fits into it like a **key into a lock**.

cards.front_md: Describe the **lock-and-key hypothesis** of enzyme action.
cards.back_md:
The **active site** has a **rigid, fixed shape** that is **complementary** to only one substrate.

The substrate fits into it like a **key into a lock**.

front_blocks.md: Describe the **induced-fit hypothesis** of enzyme action.

back_blocks.md: The **active site** is **flexible**, not rigid.
As the substrate binds, the active site **changes shape slightly** to fit more closely around it.

cards.front_md: Describe the **induced-fit hypothesis** of enzyme action.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Enzymes are changed permanently by the reactions they catalyse.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Enzymes lower the **activation energy** and remain **unchanged**, so they can be **reused**.

**True or False?**

front_blocks.md: Define the **lock-and-key hypothesis**.

back_blocks.md: A model in which the **substrate** is **complementary** in shape to the **active site** and fits into it like a **key into a lock**.

cards.front_md: Define the **lock-and-key hypothesis**.
cards.back_md: A model in which the **substrate** is **complementary** in shape to the **active site** and fits into it like a **key into a lock**.

front_blocks.md: Define the **induced-fit hypothesis**.

back_blocks.md: A model in which the **active site** is not exactly complementary at first, but **changes shape** slightly to fit closely around the substrate.

cards.front_md: Define the **induced-fit hypothesis**.
cards.back_md: A model in which the **active site** is not exactly complementary at first, but **changes shape** slightly to fit closely around the substrate.

front_blocks.md: How does the **induced-fit** hypothesis differ from the **lock-and-key** hypothesis?

back_blocks.md: In **lock-and-key**, the active site is **already complementary** to the substrate.
In **induced-fit**, the active site **moulds/changes shape** around the substrate as it binds.

cards.front_md: How does the **induced-fit** hypothesis differ from the **lock-and-key** hypothesis?
cards.back_md:
In **lock-and-key**, the active site is **already complementary** to the substrate.

In **induced-fit**, the active site **moulds/changes shape** around the substrate as it binds.

front_blocks.md: In the induced-fit model, what happens to the active site when the substrate binds?

back_blocks.md: It **changes shape** to fit more closely around the substrate, forming an **enzyme-substrate complex**.

cards.front_md: In the induced-fit model, what happens to the active site when the substrate binds?

front_blocks.md: What are the two general ways to measure the progress of an enzyme-catalysed reaction?

back_blocks.md: Measure the **rate of formation of product**, or the **rate of disappearance of substrate**.

cards.front_md: What are the two general ways to measure the progress of an enzyme-catalysed reaction?
cards.back_md: Measure the **rate of formation of product**, or the **rate of disappearance of substrate**.

front_blocks.md: How can the activity of **catalase** be measured?

back_blocks.md: By measuring the **rate of formation of product** — the **volume of oxygen** produced from the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide.

cards.front_md: How can the activity of **catalase** be measured?
cards.back_md: By measuring the **rate of formation of product** — the **volume of oxygen** produced from the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide.

front_blocks.md: How can the activity of **amylase** be measured?

back_blocks.md: By measuring the **rate of disappearance of substrate** — how quickly **starch** is broken down.

cards.front_md: How can the activity of **amylase** be measured?
cards.back_md: By measuring the **rate of disappearance of substrate** — how quickly **starch** is broken down.

front_blocks.md: Define **enzyme activity**.

back_blocks.md: The **rate** at which an enzyme converts **substrate** into **product**.

cards.front_md: Define **enzyme activity**.
cards.back_md: The **rate** at which an enzyme converts **substrate** into **product**.

front_blocks.md: Catalase activity can be measured by collecting the <u>    </u> gas produced.

front_blocks.md: When using amylase and starch, how can the end of the reaction be detected?

back_blocks.md: When **iodine solution** no longer turns **blue-black**, showing that all the **starch** has been digested.

front_blocks.md: Define **colorimeter**.

back_blocks.md: A device that measures the **absorbance** (or transmission) of light passing through a **coloured solution**.

front_blocks.md: When is a **colorimeter** useful for measuring the progress of an enzyme-catalysed reaction?

back_blocks.md: When the reaction involves a **colour change**.

front_blocks.md: How does a colorimeter measure the progress of such a reaction?

back_blocks.md: It measures the change in **absorbance** of light as the **colour** of the solution changes over time.

front_blocks.md: Why is a **calibration curve** produced before using a colorimeter?
